title: Analog Scaling and Alarms with Deadband
oneLiner: Turning raw analog counts into engineering units without integer-division bugs, catching a broken 4 to 20 mA loop, and alarms and pump control that don't chatter, using deadband, hysteresis and on-delays.
keyTakeaway: Scale with REAL arithmetic (convert first), clamp slightly out-of-range values, and treat a signal far below 4 mA as a fault, not a reading. Give alarms a deadband or an on-delay, and on/off control two switching points, so a noisy signal can't make them chatter.
explanation:
An analog input card turns a continuous signal, most often a 4 to 20 mA current loop or a 0 to 10 V voltage, into an integer called raw counts. The Digital vs. Analog I/O lesson explained the signal; this lesson is about turning counts into something useful in the program: engineering units, such as bar or degrees, and alarms.

Scaling is a straight-line conversion between two ranges. The two details that cause most bugs are integer division (in ST, 13824 / 27648 is 0, so convert to REAL before dividing) and what to do when the signal is outside its range. Slightly under or over range is usually clamped, while far below 4 mA means a broken wire or a failed transmitter, which should raise a fault rather than pass a meaningless number on.

Alarms compare a value against a limit. A plain comparison chatters, switching on and off many times a second when the value hovers near the limit. A deadband fixes that: the alarm turns on at one level and turns off only after the value has moved back past a second level. The same idea in control is called hysteresis, as in a pump that starts at 20 % and stops at 80 %. An on-delay timer is the other common cure: alarm only if the condition lasts.
